newsitem.title: GERMANY: Schering sees dividend rising in coming yrs.
newsitem.headline: Schering sees dividend rising in coming yrs.

text.p: German drugs group Schering AG expects to keep raising its dividend in the coming years if earnings continue to rise, its chief financial officer said in a newspaper interview published on Wednesday.
The company has already said it plans to raise the dividend payout to two marks ($1.25) per five-mark share for 1996 from 1.55 marks previously.

"I think the current rise in the dividend is no one-off occurrence, and that with rising profits in the coming years we will be able to change the dividend accordingly," Handelsblatt quoted Klaus Pohle as saying.

Pohle also said Schering was considering acquisitions in the field of oncology -- cancer therapy -- where Schering has formed an alliance with Hamburg-based Medac GmbH. Schering has about 1.7 billion marks in liquidity, Pohle said.

Pohle predicted earnings would show "single digit" percentage growth in 1997, a slowdown in earnings growth in 1996, due to writedowns of 70 million marks on the acquisition of Jenapharm and the Finnish Leiras group.
From 1998 on earnings would benefit from the effect of rationalisation, he added.

Asked to comment on Schering's full year 1996 results, Pohle said there was no reason to doubt previous forecasts for a 34 percent rise in net profit to about 340 million marks and sales of 5.2 billion marks.
Pohle also sought to dampen recurring speculation that Schering may become a takeover target. Any buyer would have to pay 12 to 15 billion marks for Schering, Pohle said.

That figure consists of Schering's market capitalisation of about nine billion marks plus a premium of between 30 and 50 percent. Such a price could only be justified if the takeover resulted in rationalisation gains of 300 to 500 million marks per year, but that was not possible at Schering, Pohle said.
Pohle added that Schering's only large shareholder was insurer Allianz AG Holding with a 10 percent stake.
The remainder of the shares were widely distributed, Pohle said.
"We want to remain independent," Pohle said.
